rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The section groups 2:24's challenge with 17:88's declaration that humans and jinn cannot produce the Qur'an's like, framing both as debate, challenge, and signs of inimitability.
rows.anchor: الْإِنْسُ وَالْجِنُّ عَلَى أَنْ يَأْتُوا

rows.speaker: الخطابي
rows.claim: Al-Khattabi says Qur'anic rhetoric is miraculous because it combines three levels of eloquence, excluding the disapproved hybrid, to achieve both grandeur and sweetness.
rows.anchor: ثم إن الخطابي في شرح فكرته في النظم المعجز، يرى من الإعجاز أن تأتي بلاغات القرآن جامعة لطبقات ثلاث متفاوتة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bint al-Shati rejects the implication that Qur'anic passages occupy lower eloquence levels: inimitability reaches the highest level, and one sura need not combine all three because the challenge concerns a single sura.
rows.anchor: أولاهما: أن فهمنا للإعجاز البياني، فوت لأعلى درجات البلاغة دون أوسطها وأدناها. والأخرى، أن هذه الدرجات الثلاث لا تجتمع

rows.speaker: الخطابي
rows.claim: Al-Khattabi was an early observer of fine semantic distinctions among Qur'anic terms often treated as synonyms, including knowledge and knowing, praise and thanks, and emancipation and manumission.
rows.anchor: وسبق "الخطابي" أيضاً إلى لمح فروق دقيقة في الدلالة، لألفاظ قرآنية جرت معاجمنا وكتب المفسرين على القول بترادفها

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses fūm as wheat; Abu Mihjan's line about cultivating fūm is cited as Arabic evidence for that sense.
rows.anchor: وسأله عن قول الله - عز وجل -: {وَفُومِهَا} ما الفوم؟ قال: الحنطة. أما سمعت قول أبي محجن الثقفي

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra says fūm in an old dialect can mean both wheat and bread; Arabs also used fawwimū lanā to mean bake for us.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء إن الفوم فيما ذُكِرَ لغة قديمة وهي الحنطة والخبز جميعاً

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reading attributed to Abdullah, thūmihā with thāʾ, means garlic and better fits lentils and onions; Arabic speakers can interchange fāʾ and thāʾ.
rows.anchor: وهي في قراءة عبد الله: "وثومِها" بالثاء، فكأنه أشبه المعنيين بالصواب لأنه مع ما يشاكله من العدس والبصل

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abu Ubayda glosses sharawhu in the story of Joseph as selling him for a paltry price; Ibn Mufarrigh's line uses sharraytu for sold.
rows.anchor: وفي مجاز القرآن لأبي عبيدة، آية البقرة 102 أي باعوا به أنفسهم. وقال ابن مفرغ الحميري

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra reads the phrase as how badly they sold their own souls; the passage uses it to illustrate the sell/buy senses of the root.
rows.anchor: في معاني تالقرآن للفراء: معناه والله أعلم، بئس ما باعوا به أنفسهم

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: In the most common usage, sharaw means sold and ishtaraw means bought; some Arab dialects use both for selling, with Tamim and Rabi'a examples and a line by Tarafa supporting the dialectal variation.
rows.anchor: وللعرب في شروا واشتروا مذهبان، فالأكثر منهما أن شروا: باعوا، واشتروا: ابتاعوا. وربما جعلوهما باعوا

rows.speaker: ابن فارس
rows.claim: Ibn Faris traces buying and selling to an underlying exchange, taking and giving; this explains why sharaytu can mean either purchase or sale.
rows.anchor: على أن "ابن فارس" في (المقاييس) ردَّ (شرى) في الشراء والبيع، إلى أصل "المماثلة: أخذاً وإعطاءً

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari treats buying misguidance for guidance and trading worldly life for the hereafter as metaphors for exchanging or giving one thing up for another.
rows.anchor: وذهب الزمخشري إلى أن: من المجاز {اشْتَرَوُا الضَّلَالَةَ بِالْهُدَى} : استبدلوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bint al-Shati notes that in substitution constructions the preposition bi enters the thing relinquished, as in exchanging the lower for the better.
rows.anchor: والقاعدة في الاستبدال، أن الباء تدخل على المتروك

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Raghib explains ḥūba as need or destitution, especially a need that can drive a person to sin.
rows.anchor: حقيقتها هي الحاجة التي تحمل صاحبها على ارتكاب الإثم. . . (المفردات)

rows.speaker: ابن الأثير
rows.claim: Ibn al-Athir says ḥawb means sin, understood as what one incurs if one does it.
rows.anchor: قال ابن الأثير في الحوبة: يعني ما يأثم به إن صنعه.

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: An alternative gloss takes ḥūba here as a mother and dependent female relatives who cannot manage without care, with an implied word for those dependents.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الحوبة ههنا: الأم والحرم اللائي لا يستغنين

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: In a report, a man asks the Prophet for permission to go on jihad; the Prophet asks whether he has dependent family, and he answers yes.
rows.anchor: وذكر الحديث أن رجلاً سأل النبي - صلى الله عليه وسلم - الإذن في الجهاد، قال: "ألك حوبة" قال: نعم

rows.speaker: ابن الأثير
rows.claim: Ibn al-Athir reads the ḥūba in the Umm Ayyub divorce report as loneliness or sin, and the prayer phrase arfaʿu ḥawbatī as my need.
rows.anchor: قال ابن الأثير في الحوبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bint al-Shati says the root's senses cluster around sin, need, and destitution; Qur'anic ḥūb specifically concerns guardians consuming orphans' property, while ithm is broader.
rows.anchor: وفي (مقاييس اللغة) أن الحاء والواو والباء "أصل واحد يتشعب إلى: إثم، أو حاجة، أو مسكنة. وكلها متقاربة"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: She sees kinship with vulnerable relatives as integral to ḥūb: sin is especially associated with wronging weak family members, a reading supported by reports about dependent kin.
rows.anchor: والقرآن قد خص الحوب بأكل الأوصياء على اليتامى أموالهم، وأطلق الإثم عاماً في أكل أموال اليتامى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Baqillani left later inimitability writers a rich rhetorical vocabulary; the Sakaki school inherited his method of placing Qur'anic examples beside human speech without distinction.
rows.anchor: وترك لمدرسة السكاكي، طريقته في التناول البلاغي: تقدم مع الشواهد من قول البشر شاهداً من القرآن، دون تفرقة أو تمييز

rows.speaker: الجرجاني
rows.claim: Al-Jurjani's fifth-century treatise addresses theological disputes over inimitability and counters those who divert the explanation from rhetoric, especially proponents of ṣarfa.
rows.anchor: والجرجاني - من القرن الخامس الهجري - يعرض في رسالته (الشافية) لقضية الإعجاز في جدل المتكلمين خصومه المذهبيين

rows.speaker: الجرجاني
rows.claim: For al-Jurjani, the challenge was to compose on any chosen subject at a level equal or close to the Qur'an's excellence; isolated words, lexical meanings, and mere matching of meter and rhyme were not the challenge.
rows.anchor: ويذهب الجرجاني إلى استحالة أن يكون التحدي بالكلم المفردة أو بمعانيها التي هي لها بوضع اللغة

rows.speaker: الجرجاني
rows.claim: Al-Jurjani defines composition as pursuing grammatical meanings and rules in the relations among words; the author identifies this nazm and arrangement as the remaining site of inimitability.
rows.anchor: ليس شيئاً غير توخي معاني النحو وأحكامه فيما بين الكلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bint al-Shati says the proposed ellipsis in the fasting verse is grammatically possible but does not follow a regular, general rule.
rows.anchor: فالحذف فيها ليس مما يطرد على قواعد النحاة، وإنما هو مما يجوز ولا يطرد

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some held that the initial fasting rule let able resident Muslims choose fasting or feeding a poor person per missed day, until it was abrogated and the concession restricted to the sick and travelers.
rows.anchor: قال بعضهم، كان ذلك في أوَّل ما فُرض الصوم، وكان من أطاقه من المقيمين

rows.speaker: آخرون
rows.claim: Other scholars told by al-Tabari held that none of the ruling was abrogated and that it remained in force from revelation until the end of time.
rows.anchor: قولَ آخرين: "لم يُنسخ ذلك ولا شيء منه. وهم حُكم مثبت مِن لَدُنْ نزلت هذه الآية إلى قيام الساعة"

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر النحاس
rows.claim: Al-Nahhas prefers abrogation; those who deny it explain the phrase as ability with hardship or as referring to people who formerly could fast.
rows.anchor: وأصح الأقوال فيها عنده "أبي جعفر النحاس"، أنها منسوخة، ومن لم يجعلها منسوخة فبمعنى يطيقونه على جهد

rows.speaker: أبو بكر الجصاص
rows.claim: Al-Jassas records three positions: abrogation, continued validity, or a rule allowing elderly people with no prospect of making up fasts to pay fidya; proponents considered that immediate fidya obligation consensual.
rows.anchor: ونقل فيها "أبو بكر الجصاص" في كتابه (أحكام القرآن) سورة البقرة، أقوالاً ثلاثة. أنها منسوخة، وغير منسوخة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Arabic root of falq means splitting; related forms describe cracks, a cleft in the earth, a palm splitting its spadix, and a peach opening around its pit.
rows.anchor: وأصل الفلق في العربية الشقُّ، والفلوق: الشقوق، والفالق: النخلة المنشقة عن الطلْع

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Raghib records several interpretations of al-falaq: dawn, rivers, or the word God taught Moses by which the sea split.
rows.anchor: وعند الراغب: قيل هو الصبح، وقيل: الأنهار، وقيل: الكلمة التي علَّمها اللهُ موسى فانفلق بها البحر

rows.speaker: ابن الأثير
rows.claim: Ibn al-Athir explains the Prophet's comparison of a true dream to the break of dawn as referring either to morning light or to dawn itself.
rows.anchor: فسره ابن الأثير بضوء الصبح وإنارته، أو هو الصبح نفسه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses khalaq as a share; Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt's line about having no share supports the sense, which occurs in the cited verses.
rows.anchor: وسأل ابن الأزرق عن قوله تعالى: {خَلَاقٍ} فقال ابن عباس: نصيب. وشاهده قول أمية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lexical examples connect ḥubuk with routes and patterns in sand, water, and stars, but also with tightly woven armor and firm creation, whose binding quality is central to the word.
rows.anchor: وهي عندهم الطرائق، في الرمل، إذا مرت به الريح الساكنة فتكسر، والماء كذلك وطرائق النجوم، والدرع محبوكة

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Raghib describes ḥubuk as pathways, understood either as visible star routes or as intelligible patterns perceived by insight, and traces the root to tightly woven cords.
rows.anchor: وقال الراغب في الحبك: الطرائق فمن الناس من تصور أنها الطرائق المحسوسة بالنجوم والمجرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bint al-Shati rejects an interpretation limited to pathways and good character because it misses the sense of firmness and tight weaving inherent in ḥubuk.
rows.anchor: لا يفيد دلالة الإحكام الملحوظة في الحبْك

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses ḥaraḍ as worn-out; transmitted versions also say diseased and languishing or ruined by severe pain, citing Tarafa's line about a patient made ill.
rows.anchor: الحرض البالي. قال: وهل كانت العرب تعرف ذلك؟

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bint al-Shati endorses linguists who deny true synonyms within one language: different forms reflect distinct nuances in speakers' minds, though identical meanings can occur across dialects.
rows.anchor: فأما أن يجئ في لغة واحدة فمحال أن يختلف اللفظان والمعنى الواحد، كما ظن كثير من النحويين واللغويين

rows.speaker: ابن جني
rows.claim: Ibn Jinni says equally frequent forms in one speaker may reflect tribal convention or an acquired dialect; if one is rarer, it is more likely borrowed, and multiple synonyms usually come from other tribes.
rows.anchor: فقال فيه "ابن جنى" في (باب الفصيح تجتمع في كلامه لغتان فصاعداً)

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses sawāʾ as justice and cites a poetic line using it for evenness or equal dealing.
rows.anchor: فقال ابن عباس: عدل. واستشهد بقول الشاعر: تَلاقَيْنا فقاضينا سواءٌ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bint al-Shati says the gloss justice is close because the root's core equality remains in straightness and balance; ʿadl tends toward legal usage, sawiyy toward rectitude, and sawāʾ toward equivalence.
rows.anchor: وتفسير سواءٍ بعدل، في آية آل عمران، قريب، ففي العدل دلالةُ المساواة الأصلية في المادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word occurs in twenty-six verses chiefly with equality-related contexts; the text also tracks forms of sawā, istawā, and the single sāwā in 18:96.
rows.anchor: وجاءت الكلمة في ست وعشرين آية، سياقها أقربُ إلى معنى المساواة. ومعها من المادة: (الصراط السوىّ)

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas interprets sawāʾ al-jaḥīm as the middle of Hell, and a cited Arabic verse supports the expression for a central place.
rows.anchor: فقال ابن عباس: في وسط الجحيم. سأله ابن الأزرق: وهل كانت العرب تعرف ذلك؟ قال: نعم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bint al-Shati derives the sense from a midpoint between endpoints: physical equality extends figuratively to a balanced word in 3:64 and to two alternatives being equal in 2:6.
rows.anchor: وتفسير الكلمة في آية الصافات بالوسط، قريب من أصل دلالة الكلمة على الموضع الوسَط بين الأطراف

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Raghib also interprets the phrase as the middle of Hell, describing a place whose two ends are equal and noting adjectival and adverbial use.
rows.anchor: ذهب الراغب كذلك إلى أن

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra likewise explains the phrase as the middle of Hell.
rows.anchor: وبالوسط فسرها الفراء في المعاني

rows.speaker: الأصمعي، وابن السكيت، وابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Al-Asma'i, Ibn al-Sikkit, and Ibn al-Anbari also discuss sawāʾ in their works on antonyms.
rows.anchor: والأصمعي وابن السكيت وابن الأنباري، في (الأضداد) لهم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses ill as kinship; the entry gives poetic evidence and notes the word occurs only here in this form and root.
rows.anchor: قال: الرحِم، قال فيه حسان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bint al-Shati notes that Arabic ill can mean covenant, oath, neighbor, or kinship; lexicographers commonly explain it as kinship, while al-Raghib includes any apparent bond of covenant or relation.
rows.anchor: ومن معاني الإِلَّ في العربية: العهد والحلف والجار والقرابة

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Al-Tabari transmits from Mujahid that ill means God.
rows.anchor: وأسند الطبري عن مجاهد من عدة طرق: أن {إِلًّا} في آية التوبة: الله

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Tabari says the verse should not be restricted to one sense: ill can encompass covenant, agreement, oath, kinship, and also God.
rows.anchor: قال الطبري: الأوْلى أن يقال إن الإِل على معان ثلاثة: العهد والعقد والحلف والقرابة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an speaks of multiple revealed laws and paths while treating religion as one; it never uses the plural adyān for religions.
rows.anchor: وتتعدد الشرائع: {لِكُلٍّ جَعَلْنَا مِنْكُمْ شِرْعَةً وَمِنْهَاجًا} والدين واحد، فليس في القرآن كله لفظ: أديان، جمعاً

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses yanʿ as ripeness and full development; a poem describing a fresh, flourishing branch supports the sense.
rows.anchor: قال: نضجه وبلاغه. واستشهد بقول الشاعر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bint al-Shati distinguishes yanʿ as the natural peak of a plant or fruit's flourishing from naḍaj, used for skins cooked by fire in the punishment passage 4:56.
rows.anchor: ولا يفوتنا معه أن الينع لأوج الأزدهار الطبيعي في النبت والثمر، على حين جاء النضج، لما تنضجه النار
